questions.q: What does the FROM clause specify?
options: The table or view the data comes from
The columns you want returned
How the results should be sorted
Which rows to filter out
questions.explain: FROM names the source table or view; SELECT names the columns you want from it.

options: Return every column, in the table's defined order
Return every table in the database
Multiply two columns together
Return only the first column
questions.explain: The asterisk is a wildcard meaning 'all columns' — useful for exploring, but rarely ideal in production code.

questions.q: In Person.Person, what does the first 'Person' refer to?
options: The schema — a named container that groups related tables
The database name
The column name
A typo — it should only be written once
questions.explain: schema.table naming means Person.Person is the Person table inside the Person schema.

questions.q: Why does this course end every statement with a semicolon?
options: It's good habit that prevents real errors once a script has more than one statement
SQL Server refuses to run a statement without one
It marks the start of a comment
It's required only for SELECT statements
questions.explain: T-SQL doesn't strictly require a trailing semicolon on the last statement in a batch, but consistent use avoids ambiguity as scripts grow.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid two-part table reference in AdventureWorks2012?
options: Sales.Currency
Currency.Sales
AdventureWorks2012.Currency
Currency(Sales)
questions.explain: Sales.Currency means the Currency table inside the Sales schema — the pattern used throughout this course.
